# AJG (Arthur J. Gallagher & Co.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand: Gallagher brokers and manages insurance and risk-management programs for commercial clients, earning commissions and fees on placements and renewals. It does not underwrite risk itself, so this is closer to an asset-light services/distribution business than an insurer. The one genuinely non-trivial judgment call is sizing up the AssuredPartners acquisition - a deal large enough to nearly double the scale of the risk-management segment - which requires assessing integration execution, not just the brokerage model itself.

## Moat & Durability — Score 8/10
The core brokerage moat is textbook: renewal-based recurring revenue (industry retention rates typically mid-90s%), no underwriting capital at risk, and real switching costs for commercial clients whose renewal cycles, claims history, and specialty placements are embedded with their incumbent broker. Scale matters too - larger brokers place business more efficiently with carriers and win access to specialty/reinsurance markets smaller shops can't reach. Gallagher's differentiator versus peers is a genuine 30+ year record of disciplined, culturally consistent tuck-in M&A that has compounded organic growth into something faster - visible here in 30.9% revenue growth, almost entirely a function of the AssuredPartners deal rather than organic expansion. That track record earns the high score, but it is being tested at a scale (the largest deal in company history) well outside the historical tuck-in pattern, which is why this isn't a 9 or 10.

## Management & Capital Allocation
Decades of small, disciplined M&A at consistent multiples is the single best piece of evidence for management quality here, and it's why the market has historically paid up for Gallagher relative to plain insurance-broker peers. The numbers this packet can see are consistent with a business absorbing a large deal: ROE of 6.7% (well below what this business earns in steady state) and debt/equity near 59%, both plausibly explained by fresh equity and debt issued to fund AssuredPartners plus step-up intangible amortization compressing reported net income. What the packet cannot show is the actual state of integration - producer retention, cross-sell progress, realized cost synergies - so 'trustworthy management' here rests on a multi-decade track record, not on visibility into the current deal's execution.

## Predictability
The brokerage model is inherently predictable - recurring commissions, low correlation to underwriting losses, a beta of 0.50 confirming defensive character in the market's own pricing. But right now the reported numbers are anything but steady: a 42.0x trailing P/E against a 16.9x forward P/E is a large gap that only makes sense if one-time deal costs and elevated intangible amortization are expected to roll off sharply, and the packet's thesis field is empty, leaving no qualitative confirmation that integration is on track. This fails Munger's 'easy decision' bar for the next several quarters, even though the steady-state business is simple.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Integration disappoints**: AssuredPartners synergies underdeliver, or producer attrition and cultural friction erode the acquired book faster than expected, keeping ROE structurally depressed rather than normalizing toward historical levels as the forward multiple assumes.
2. **Insurance pricing cycle turns**: a softening commercial P&C rate environment compresses organic commission growth precisely when the company is carrying its highest-ever leverage (debt/equity ~59%) from deal financing, squeezing free cash flow available for deleveraging.
3. **Price already embeds the good outcome**: the current valuation (42x trailing, 16.9x forward) is a bet that normalized earnings materialize close to consensus; if actual normalized EPS lands closer to the depressed trailing run-rate, the market has ample room to re-rate the stock down even without any operational miss.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($64.4B), trailing P/E (42.0x), forward P/E (16.9x), EV/EBITDA (18.1x), and FCF yield (3.2%) but no share price or share count directly. Using an approximate ~245M diluted share count (a modeling assumption reflecting post-deal equity issuance, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $263, trailing EPS near $6.26, forward EPS near $15.58, and FCF/share near $8.49. The trailing-to-forward EPS gap (~2.5x) is unusually wide even for a business absorbing a large acquisition, so I haircut the forward consensus rather than accept it outright, landing on normalized owner earnings of roughly $10-12/share once deal-related noise is stripped out but integration risk is still priced in.

Applying a quality-brokerage multiple range (18x-22x, roughly Gallagher's own historical forward-multiple band, rather than the market's currently implied 16.9x or the depressed 42x trailing figure):
- **Low case**: 18x × ~$10.8/share ≈ $195/share
- **High case**: 22x × ~$11.1/share ≈ $245/share

Midpoint ~$220/share against an implied current price of ~$263/share gives a margin of safety of roughly -16%. That is not a table-pounding discount - it's a good business priced for a lot of the AssuredPartners normalization to go right, with limited cushion if it goes only partly right.

## The Cloning Caveat
Glenn Greenberg's Brave Warrior Advisors (formerly Chieftain Capital) opened a brand-new position sized at 6.43% of the portfolio - a real signal, since Greenberg runs one of the most concentrated, selective books in the value-investing world and rarely holds more than a handful of names at a time. That is genuine corroboration of the moat/quality thesis, not a token allocation. First Pacific Advisors added aggressively (+244.7% shares) though the resulting stake is a moderate 2.73% of portfolio, and also opened a smaller 1.2% new position the prior quarter - building conviction, not full conviction. Dodge & Cox (two separate adds, still under 1% combined) and Mairs & Power (0.66% new position) round out basket-level exposure; Ariel's 0.01% add is immaterial. Read together: a genuinely selective concentrated investor plus several generalist value shops are converging on the name, which supports the moat and management assessment - but none of them, including Greenberg, is betting the price is a screaming bargain at 40%+ of a fund. Corroboration for the business quality, not a substitute for the valuation math above.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 5/10.** Gallagher is an excellent, understandable, historically well-run business with a real and durable moat, but it just completed the largest acquisition in its history and the packet's own numbers (a 42x-vs-17x P/E gap, 6.7% ROE, ~59% debt/equity) show a company mid-digestion, not mid-compounding. The implied current price already prices in a fairly complete normalization of that deal's earnings drag, leaving a negative margin of safety against a conservative owner-earnings estimate. Glenn Greenberg's new position is a genuine quality signal worth taking seriously, but it argues for watching closely through the next few quarters of integration data - or waiting for a better entry price - rather than buying today.
momentum_thesis: AJG is mid-recovery, not extended: a -12.1% 12-month return has been mostly clawed back by a +27.7% 3-month and +18.9% 6-month rally, while RSI14 sits neutral at 48.1 and price is only 8.0% above the 200DMA — no sign of a blow-off top, and the flat -1.0% 1-month print reads as digestion after the sprint rather than a rollover. Positioning offers little squeeze fuel (2.47% short float, 3.91 days to cover) so this is a fundamentals/flow-driven move, not a technical one, and the sub-1 put/call OI ratio (0.48) shows options flow leaning bullish without looking stretched. The real signal is the buy list: Glenn Greenberg (Brave Warrior) opened a fresh 6.43%-of-portfolio position in Q2 2026, First Pacific Advisors built a position across two consecutive quarters (new in Q1, +244.7% shares in Q2), and Dodge & Cox added in both Q1 (+735% shares) and Q2 (+27%) — that's patient, valuation-sensitive capital accumulating through the drawdown and into the recovery, which is exactly the kind of durable bid that can underwrite a low-beta (0.502) name's next leg rather than a momentum-chase set up to fade. Net: this looks like early-stage trend repair with a real fundamental sponsor base behind it, still with room to run before RSI or the 200DMA spread flags exhaustion.
